threatModel.summary: Real Fabric is a ten-minute conference-stage demo in which a React/Vite browser creates or joins an open room through a Cloudflare Worker, receives a participant rejoin credential and a provisioned relay credential, opens an authenticated control-plane WebSocket to a per-room SQLite Durable Object, and publishes or subscribes to independent audio tracks through MoqTransportAdapter and a Cloudflare WebTransport/MOQT relay. There is no live AI pipeline; AI behaviour is labelled presenter simulation. Production and declared staging select MOQT draft 16, cooperative routing, unknown discovery and an unverified transport claim (wrangler.jsonc:3-30,37-48; src/client/session/RoomSession.ts:241-320; src/worker/index.ts:77-143).
assets: Raw microphone audio, Opus frames and decoded PCM, kept in browser memory/worklets and not persisted by application source (src/client/audio/CaptureController.ts:34-43,62-115,147-170; public/audio/mixer-worklet.js:23-67).

The provisioned MOQ_RELAY_TOKEN and its coarse relay publish/subscribe authority, returned to every creator or joiner and appended to the WebTransport URL path (src/worker/env.ts:16-25; src/worker/index.ts:98-143,289-304; src/client/transport/MoqTransportAdapter.ts:225-271,532-540).
Participant identity and control authority: room code, participant ID, rejoin token/hash, role, state and routing ownership (src/client/api.ts:10-17,200-230; src/worker/room.ts:45-68,148-180).
Room-state integrity for membership, routing, AI pipeline/floor, simulation, AI-to-AI turns, expiry and reconnect deadlines (src/worker/room.ts:70-84,535-594,820-855).
Privacy of display names and routing relationships in a complete RoomSnapshot readable by a room-code holder (src/shared/contracts.ts:51-78,126-138; src/worker/index.ts:117-143).

Relay-visible track namespace integrity: demo/<room-code>/<participant-id>/audio/<participant-id>, not independently bound to a participant by the shared credential (src/shared/tracks.ts:17-40; src/client/session/RoomSession.ts:544-580).

Availability controls: creation throttling, room expiry, AI turn cap and bounded simulation counts; concurrent-room, credential-issuance and AI-cost ceilings are absent (src/shared/contracts.ts:24-35; src/worker/room.ts:114-138,383-430; PRODUCT_SPEC_v1-demo_1.md:17-31).
Sanitised telemetry, application logs and privileged Cloudflare build/deployment authority (src/client/telemetry/SessionTelemetry.ts:15-81; src/worker/index.ts:33-73,382-389; package.json:8-18).
trustBoundaries: Unauthenticated Internet caller to Worker API: health and creation are public; joining is open with a room code; full snapshots are readable with the room code; field validation follows whole-body parsing (src/worker/index.ts:77-143; src/worker/validation.ts:11-105).

Participant browser to Durable Object: mutations carry participantId and rejoinToken; routing binds its row to the authenticated participant, while AI, floor, AI-to-AI and presenter operations require only any human role (src/worker/room.ts:272-452,785-810).

Participant browser to control WebSocket: the reusable token is placed in a same-origin query string and authenticated before socket acceptance; only ping/pong client messages are accepted (src/client/api.ts:187-198; src/worker/index.ts:263-280; src/worker/room.ts:466-533).

Worker secret to browser and relay: the same optional secret is returned raw at create/join, held in memory and encoded into the relay URL path (src/worker/relayCredential.ts:1-13; src/worker/index.ts:98-143,289-304; src/client/transport/MoqTransportAdapter.ts:532-597).

Relay-originated setup and media objects to moqtail, TrackPlayer, jitter/deduplication buffers, decoder and mixer; dependency internals and relay are outside the inventory (src/client/transport/MoqTransportAdapter.ts:1-18,307-471; src/client/audio/TrackPlayer.ts:72-136).
Developer/CI principal to Cloudflare deployment through pinned Wrangler; account and approval are external (package.json:8-18; wrangler.jsonc:1-16).
attackerCapabilities: An unauthenticated caller can create a limited number of rooms and join any known room code, but lacks another participant token and deployment credentials (src/worker/index.ts:77-143,327-344).
A room-code holder can read the complete RoomSnapshot without joining (src/worker/index.ts:117-143; src/shared/contracts.ts:126-138).

A joined human receives a reusable participant credential and the configured shared relay token; their participant credential authorises all AI, floor, AI-to-AI and presenter operations because the backend checks only human role (src/worker/index.ts:155-260; src/worker/room.ts:187-452).

A shared relay-token holder gains the externally configured coarse authority; source implements no per-room, participant or track grant and labels routing cooperative (src/worker/index.ts:289-304; src/worker/room.ts:916-920).
A malicious participant publisher or compromised relay can supply setup and media objects to the browser receive path (src/client/transport/MoqTransportAdapter.ts:225-471).
securityObjectives: Keep credentials out of share links, snapshots, telemetry and application logs, and issue only short-lived least-privilege relay authority (src/shared/contracts.ts:140-154; src/client/api.ts:187-219; src/client/telemetry/SessionTelemetry.ts:24-81).

Preserve routing ownership and distinguish ordinary participant authority from presenter/global room authority; never claim relay enforcement while credentials are coarse (src/worker/room.ts:267-452,916-920).
Bound request, room, WebSocket and media-object resources without imposing a legitimate participant-count cap (src/shared/contracts.ts:24-35; src/worker/room.ts:114-138,499-525).

Validate identifiers and input; store only token hashes and require matching active participant credentials (src/worker/index.ts:117-123,306-344; src/worker/validation.ts:11-105; src/worker/room.ts:793-810,1035-1045).

Keep microphone audio transient and close capture, worklets, publications, subscriptions and sockets on leave (src/client/audio/CaptureController.ts:147-170; src/client/session/RoomSession.ts:995-1019).
Bind privileged deployment to the intended account, Worker, environment, revision and payload externally (package.json:8-18; wrangler.jsonc:1-16).

No SECURITY.md, supplied threat model, user security context or authoritative knowledge base was available.
Docs say the relay token is configured and expires on 2026-09-01, but source proves only an optional secret reference (README.md:85-92; src/worker/env.ts:16-25).
The Product Spec calls the rejoin token single-use, but source reuses it unchanged after reclaim (PRODUCT_SPEC_v1-demo_1.md:195-201; src/worker/room.ts:596-630,793-810).

The Product Spec calls several operations presenter actions and says each human sees only their routing row, while server authorisation is any human and snapshots contain all rows (PRODUCT_SPEC_v1-demo_1.md:226-237,263-273; src/worker/room.ts:383-452,820-855).
moqtail internals, generated dist, relay, Cloudflare platform logging and deployed bindings are outside the authorised inventory.

findings.title: Room creation and joining disclose a relay-wide publish/subscribe bearer
findings.summary: The public create route and open join route return the same configured MOQ_RELAY_TOKEN to browsers. The adapter then authenticates relay operations with that bearer without room, participant, track, action or expiry claims.

severity.rationale: A public caller can obtain authority intended to publish and subscribe at the relay, bypassing all client-only routing controls. This compromises the primary media isolation boundary if the configured relay accepts the documented token authority.

confidence.rationale: The unscoped credential flow and caller-controlled adapter operations are direct source facts. Actual relay acceptance, ACLs, expiry and duplicate-publication semantics remain unverified.

codeEvidence.label: Worker returns the configured token
codeEvidence.explanation: The application explicitly describes relay-wide authority and returns the configured secret unchanged.

codeEvidence.label: Public create response includes the bearer
codeEvidence.explanation: Room creation requires no existing participant authority yet returns the relay bearer.

rootCause.summary: A single Worker secret is treated as a browser credential; no server component mints or enforces room-, participant-, publication- or subscription-specific claims.

findings.remediation: Replace the shared browser-visible token with short-lived credentials scoped to one opaque room and participant, authorising only the participant's publication track and server-approved subscriptions. If the relay cannot enforce that scope, keep live transport unavailable or add an enforcing relay boundary, then rotate the shared secret.

assertions: Both create and join return relayCredential(env).
configuredRelayCredential returns the trimmed Worker secret unchanged.
MoqTransportAdapter accepts caller-selected publication, subscription and namespace targets.
counterEvidence: Responses are no-store; the token is absent from RoomSnapshot, logs and telemetry.
Room codes and participant identifiers are high entropy.
Routing is truthfully labelled cooperative and transport is unverified.
limitations: Successful relay abuse was not run because live relay acceptance is outside the authorised source snapshot.

attackPath.summary: An Internet caller creates a room, receives the global relay bearer, and uses a modified client to request relay operations outside application routing.

remediationTests: Verify create and join return distinct short-lived credentials.
Attempt publication outside the participant's own namespace and assert relay denial.
Toggle routing consent and assert a revoked subscription is rejected at the relay.
preventiveControls: Automated check forbidding Worker secret passthrough into API responses.
Credential claims and expiry audit logging without token values.
Live relay acceptance tests for namespace ownership and revocation.

originalCandidates.rule: A Worker-wide relay bearer credential is disclosed to every room creator and joiner
originalCandidates.attacker: Any unauthenticated Internet user who creates a room, or any person who joins a known room.
originalCandidates.violated_security_invariant: Relay credentials must be short-lived and least-privilege, with participant publication and subscription authority enforced.
originalCandidates.source_to_sink: Unauthenticated create and open join handlers include relayCredential(env); that helper returns the same trimmed MOQ_RELAY_TOKEN without room, participant, track, action or expiry scoping; the browser inserts it into the relay WebTransport URL.
originalCandidates.impact: If accepted with the documented coarse authority, a modified client can bypass cooperative routing, subscribe or publish outside UI permissions, impersonate tracks and disrupt participants.
supporting_source_evidence: Creation needs no participant credential yet returns the Worker relay secret.
The same secret is returned for creation and every join.
No source mints participant- or room-specific grants or derives relay permissions from routing.
counterevidence: The token is a Worker secret and omitted from logs, telemetry, snapshots and share links.
Identifiers are opaque and UI labels routing cooperative.
Live relay acceptance and deployed scope are unverified.
originalCandidates.recommended_remediation: Mint short-lived room/participant credentials restricting publication and subscriptions; revoke them on routing, leave and expiry; do not expose a relay-wide secret if enforcement is unavailable.

findings.title: Any joined human can execute presenter and AI lifecycle controls
findings.summary: All AI creation, removal, pipeline, presenter-simulation and AI-to-AI administration methods authorise through assertHuman, which distinguishes only human from AI. The server stores no creator, presenter, owner or per-AI worker authority.

severity.rationale: An ordinary attendee can corrupt or remove the complete AI cast, change global safety state and interrupt the ten-minute stage demonstration for every participant.

confidence.rationale: The public routes, Durable Object mutations and shared assertHuman guard are directly visible, and the product specification explicitly identifies presenter-only operations.

codeEvidence.label: AI creation accepts any human
codeEvidence.explanation: The only authority check for creating room-wide AIs is membership as any human.

codeEvidence.label: Shared guard has no presenter role
codeEvidence.explanation: The central guard cannot distinguish the room creator, presenter, AI worker or an ordinary attendee.

rootCause.summary: Global room mutations rely on a role predicate that verifies only human membership, while presenterMode is client-side UI state and no stronger server principal exists.

findings.remediation: Persist a room owner/presenter capability at creation, support deliberate delegation, require it for presenter and AI lifecycle administration, and issue per-AI worker credentials for pipeline heartbeats. Add per-room AI mutation and cost budgets without capping ordinary human membership.

assertions: A second joined human receives a credential accepted by addAi, removeAi, setAiPipeline, setAiToAi and configurePresenter.
No owner/presenter field or capability is persisted.
Client sessionStorage changes only UI visibility.
counterEvidence: A valid high-entropy participant credential is required.
Simulation counts and AI-to-AI turns are bounded.
Rooms hard-stop after twenty minutes and no live AI workers exist yet.
limitations: External AI cost impact is prospective because the revision uses labelled presenter simulation only.

attackPath.summary: A room-code holder joins normally, then sends global mutation requests with their own participant credential; assertHuman authorises each operation and the Durable Object broadcasts the altered state.

remediationTests: Create a room, join a second human, and assert 403 for every global presenter/AI operation.
Assert a valid presenter capability succeeds and can be revoked.
Assert per-AI credentials can update only their bound AI pipeline.
preventiveControls: Central authorisation policy for room-global actions.
Negative cross-participant tests for every new RPC.
Explicit AI lifecycle and cost budgets.

originalCandidates.rule: Any joined human can execute presenter-only global room controls
originalCandidates.attacker: Any attendee who knows the room code and joins normally.
originalCandidates.violated_security_invariant: Global presenter actions must be authorised to a presenter or owner, not any human.
originalCandidates.source_to_sink: All AI, floor, AI-to-AI and presenter mutations call assertHuman, which verifies only human role; the browser presenter flag affects only UI visibility, and requestFloor accepts arbitrary aiId.
originalCandidates.impact: A malicious attendee can add/remove AIs, fabricate pipeline state, reconfigure simulation, enable AI loops or wedge floor ownership.
supporting_source_evidence: Open membership gives every attendee a valid human credential.
No owner or presenter role is persisted or checked.
Every global action accepts any valid human credential.
counterevidence: Anonymous, invalid-token and AI-role callers are rejected.
originalCandidates.recommended_remediation: Persist a room owner/presenter principal and require a distinct server capability for global mutations; validate AI targets; limit ordinary humans to participant-owned operations.

findings.title: Unvalidated AI identifiers can wedge or pre-empt the global floor
findings.summary: requestFloor stores an arbitrary caller-supplied aiId as the floor holder or queue entry without proving that it names an active AI. releaseFloor likewise needs only the supplied holder ID.

severity.rationale: A joined human can block every legitimate AI behind a nonexistent holder, fill the queue with bogus identifiers or release another AI's turn, disrupting shared room availability.

confidence.rationale: The missing target lookup and direct SQL writes are explicit in source; no foreign key or turn capability exists.

codeEvidence.label: Caller target is stored without validation
codeEvidence.explanation: No participant existence, role or state check occurs before the supplied identifier becomes shared floor state.

rootCause.summary: The floor API trusts an identifier asserted by a human caller and the database schema does not bind floor holders or queue entries to active AI participant rows.

findings.remediation: Resolve aiId to an active role='ai' participant before every floor operation. Bind acquisition and release to an authorised AI or server-issued turn capability, reject stale requests and constrain the queue to active AI rows.

assertions: Nonexistent and human identifiers are accepted as floor holders.
releaseFloor has no proof that the caller controls the active AI turn.
floor_queue has only a text primary key.
counterEvidence: A valid human credential is required.
Duplicate queue identifiers are deduplicated.
Removing a known AI cleans its own floor state.

controls: A valid human credential is required.
Duplicate queue identifiers are deduplicated.

impact.rationale: Shared AI turn-taking is wedged or pre-empted until another caller supplies the exact bogus holder or the room expires.

preconditions: The attacker is an active human participant.
steps: Join as a human.
Request the floor for a nonexistent identifier while the floor is empty.
Legitimate AIs subsequently queue behind the unreachable holder.
attackPath.summary: An ordinary human calls the floor route with a fabricated or known aiId; the Durable Object stores or releases that identifier without target validation.

remediationTests: Reject nonexistent, human, left and simulated-disallowed targets.
Require a valid turn capability to release the holder.
Verify queue rows reference active AI participants after lifecycle changes.
preventiveControls: Foreign-key or application invariant for floor targets.
Invariant tests for every participant state transition.

originalCandidates.rule: Unvalidated floor targets let any human wedge or pre-empt the global AI floor
originalCandidates.violated_security_invariant: Floor holders and queued entries must be active AIs and release must prove control of the turn.
originalCandidates.source_to_sink: requestFloor writes caller-supplied aiId to floor holder or queue after assertHuman without participant lookup. releaseFloor clears or advances when the supplied ID equals the holder.
originalCandidates.impact: A participant can wedge the floor with nonexistent/human IDs, queue bogus IDs, or pre-empt another AI's active floor.
supporting_source_evidence: No role/state/existence validation precedes writes.
floor_queue has no foreign key.
Release needs only holder ID knowledge.
counterevidence: Known AI removal cleans that AI's state.
originalCandidates.recommended_remediation: Require an active AI target and bind acquire/release to a server-side turn or authorised AI capability.

findings.title: Public room snapshots disclose every human's per-AI routing preferences
findings.summary: The unauthenticated room snapshot selects and serialises all routing rows, including who permits each AI to hear them and who listens to each AI. Join responses and control WebSockets reuse the same complete snapshot.

severity.rationale: A room-code holder can map display names and participant IDs to individual consent/listening choices that the binding product specification says are owner-only.

confidence.rationale: The public GET route, unrestricted routing query and returned contract are direct source facts, and the privacy requirement is explicit.

codeEvidence.label: Snapshot returns every routing row
codeEvidence.explanation: The snapshot has no viewer context and therefore cannot filter detailed rows to their owner.

rootCause.summary: One viewer-independent RoomSnapshot is used for public HTTP, join and WebSocket responses even though routing preferences contain per-human private consent state.

findings.remediation: Create separate public and participant-specific snapshots. Authenticate detailed routing reads, return only rows owned by the caller, and expose a server-computed aggregate 'Partial context' state for everyone else.

assertions: GET by room code requires no participant credential.
snapshot executes SELECT * FROM routing.
toRouting exposes humanId, aiId, hearsMe and iHearIt.
counterEvidence: The room code is high entropy and acts as a share capability.
Tokens and relay credentials are absent.
Room state expires after twenty minutes.

originalCandidates.rule: Public room snapshots disclose every human's private per-AI routing row
originalCandidates.violated_security_invariant: Each human may see only their own detailed routing row; others receive aggregate context.
originalCandidates.source_to_sink: Unauthenticated GET returns getSnapshot; snapshot selects every routing row and serialises humanId, aiId, hearsMe and iHearIt. The same full snapshot is returned at join and over every WebSocket.
originalCandidates.impact: A room-code holder can map names and IDs to each person's AI listening and consent choices, contrary to the product's row-visibility promise.
supporting_source_evidence: HTTP snapshot has no credential.

originalCandidates.recommended_remediation: Split public and participant-specific snapshots; authenticate detailed routing; return only the caller's rows; expose only server-computed aggregate context for others.

findings.title: A reusable participant bearer is placed in the WebSocket query string
findings.summary: roomEventsUrl appends the participant's general rejoin token to the WebSocket URL. The Worker and Durable Object read that query value for authentication, and reclaim returns the same reusable token without consumption or rotation.

severity.rationale: If an intermediary, diagnostic or access log captures the handshake URL, its reader can replay the participant's general credential for sockets and mutation APIs during the room lifetime.

confidence.rationale: URL placement and token reuse are direct source facts, while actual external query-string logging is deployment-dependent and was not established.

codeEvidence.label: Client embeds reusable bearer in URL
codeEvidence.explanation: The code explicitly treats the URL as secret but places the reusable general bearer in it.

rootCause.summary: The socket handshake reuses a general-purpose participant credential instead of exchanging it through an authenticated request for a purpose-bound, single-use socket ticket.

findings.remediation: Add an authenticated endpoint that mints a very short-lived, participant- and room-bound socket ticket. Consume it atomically on the first upgrade, never put the rejoin token in a URL, and rotate the rejoin credential after successful reclaim.

assertions: The complete token is appended as token=.
The same token authenticates other participant mutations.
Reclaim does not consume or rotate it.
counterEvidence: Application logs normalise to pathname and omit queries.
TLS protects transit.
The token is random, hashed at rest and bounded by leave or room expiry.
limitations: Cloudflare or proxy full-URL logging was not verified.

originalCandidates.rule: A reusable participant bearer token is placed in the WebSocket URL query string
originalCandidates.attacker: A party able to read handshake URLs from diagnostics, platform/proxy logs, monitoring or support artefacts.
originalCandidates.violated_security_invariant: Reusable authentication secrets must not be placed in URLs commonly recorded by infrastructure.
originalCandidates.source_to_sink: roomEventsUrl appends participant ID and reusable rejoin token; Worker and Durable Object authenticate with that query token; reclaim returns it unchanged.
originalCandidates.impact: A disclosed URL permits participant impersonation, event access and authenticated mutations.
supporting_source_evidence: The URL contains the bearer used for HTTP mutations.

originalCandidates.recommended_remediation: Exchange the main credential for a single-use short-expiry socket ticket and rotate the rejoin credential on reclaim.

findings.title: One participant token can open unbounded concurrent control sockets
findings.summary: Every authenticated events upgrade creates and retains another WebSocket, sends a full snapshot and includes it in every later broadcast. The participant tag is never used to enforce a per-participant concurrency bound.

severity.rationale: A single participant can amplify Durable Object connection, serialisation and broadcast work until the control plane becomes unavailable during the demo.

confidence.rationale: The upgrade allocation and broadcast iteration are direct source paths; no local throttle, ticket consumption or concurrency check exists.

codeEvidence.label: Each token replay allocates another socket
codeEvidence.explanation: The participant tag is recorded but not checked against existing sockets.

rootCause.summary: The reusable participant credential is accepted independently for every upgrade and no per-participant connection ownership or bounded reconnect policy is enforced.

findings.remediation: Use single-use socket tickets, enforce one active socket or a small documented bound per participant, close or replace the older socket on reconnect, rate-limit upgrades and bound initial snapshot/broadcast work.

assertions: The same credential can authenticate repeated upgrades.
Each upgrade serialises and sends a full snapshot.
broadcast sends to every retained socket.
counterEvidence: A valid active participant credential is required.
Only ping messages are accepted from clients.
Room expiry closes sockets and platform quotas may cap absolute scale.
limitations: Cloudflare connection ceilings were not inspected.

originalCandidates.attacker: A malicious participant or credential-replay attacker.
originalCandidates.violated_security_invariant: Control connections must be bounded per participant and room.
originalCandidates.source_to_sink: Every authenticated upgrade creates and retains a new WebSocket, sends a full snapshot and receives every later broadcast. No existing-socket check, ticket consumption, throttle or concurrency cap exists.
originalCandidates.impact: One participant can consume Durable Object socket resources and amplify full-snapshot and broadcast work across attacker sockets.
supporting_source_evidence: Participant tags are not used for limits.

originalCandidates.recommended_remediation: Use single-use tickets; enforce one or a small bound of sockets per participant; rate-limit upgrades and bound initial snapshot/broadcast work.

findings.title: Unthrottled open-room joins permit unbounded participant and routing allocation
findings.summary: The open join path has no source- or room-level rate limit. Every non-reclaim join inserts a participant, seeds routing for every AI, broadcasts and serialises a complete snapshot; the Worker also fetched a snapshot immediately before joining.

severity.rationale: A room-code holder can grow participant and human-by-AI routing state and amplify snapshots/broadcasts fast enough to degrade or exhaust a room Durable Object.

confidence.rationale: The absence of a join limiter and the per-join allocations are explicit. The product's no-participant-cap rule does not prohibit velocity limits.

codeEvidence.label: Each request creates persistent participant state
codeEvidence.explanation: Every fresh join performs persistent writes, cross-product routing work, a broadcast and a growing snapshot.

rootCause.summary: Only room creation is throttled; open membership was implemented without a separate abuse-velocity and credential-issuance budget.

findings.remediation: Add per-source and per-room token-bucket join limits with documented burst capacity and Retry-After. Rate-limit relay credential issuance separately, avoid duplicate snapshot serialisation, and budget routing-row creation while preserving the no-participant-count-cap requirement.

assertions: No join limiter is invoked.
Each new human creates routing rows for all active AIs.
Every join broadcasts and returns the full snapshot.
counterEvidence: The attacker must know a high-entropy room code.
Input lengths and room lifetime are bounded.
Membership intentionally has no count cap.
limitations: Cloudflare object and request ceilings were not measured.

findings.title: Worker parses unbounded JSON bodies before rate limiting or authentication
findings.summary: readJsonObject calls request.json() after checking only Content-Type. Field validation, the room-creation limiter and participant authentication all occur after the entire attacker-controlled body has been buffered and parsed.

severity.rationale: Unauthenticated or invalid-credential callers can impose disproportionate Worker CPU and memory cost with bodies far larger than the expected sub-kilobyte schemas.

confidence.rationale: The ordering and absence of any declared-length or streaming byte bound are directly visible.

codeEvidence.label: Whole body parsed without byte limit
codeEvidence.explanation: No application body ceiling is checked before the full parse.

rootCause.summary: The shared JSON helper treats platform request limits as the only byte bound and the route ordering performs cheap admission controls only after parsing.

findings.remediation: Enforce a small application-specific byte ceiling before JSON.parse using both declared Content-Length and a streaming counter. Run creation rate limiting before reading the body and authenticate mutations before parsing where feasible.

assertions: No Content-Length ceiling, streamed counter or 413 path exists.
Creation parses before enforceCreationRateLimit.
Mutation bodies parse before Durable Object credential verification.
counterEvidence: Non-JSON Content-Type is rejected.
Join checks room existence first.
Cloudflare limits make each request finite; fields are bounded after parsing.
limitations: No runtime memory or CPU threshold was measured.
validation.method: Offline source review of the exact authorised Git revision.

impact.rationale: Repeated requests can consume isolate CPU/memory, increase cost and disrupt room control endpoints.

steps: Send application/json with a body much larger than the legitimate schema.

attackPath.summary: An unauthenticated caller sends oversized JSON to a public or credentialed route; the Worker buffers and parses it before the request is rate-limited or rejected.

remediationTests: Reject declared bodies above 8 KiB with 413 before parsing.
Stream a chunked body beyond the cap and assert termination.
Verify creation limiting runs before body consumption.
preventiveControls: Worker CPU and rejected-body-size telemetry without logging payloads.

originalCandidates.rule: Untrusted JSON bodies are fully allocated and parsed before application size and rate controls
originalCandidates.attacker: Any unauthenticated caller of room creation and callers reaching mutation routes.
originalCandidates.violated_security_invariant: Untrusted bodies must be bounded before whole-body allocation and cheap admission controls should precede parsing.
originalCandidates.source_to_sink: readJsonObject immediately awaits request.json(); field validation and the creation limiter run only after parsing.
originalCandidates.impact: Oversized or deeply structured bodies can consume Worker CPU/memory before rejection.
supporting_source_evidence: No Content-Length ceiling or bounded reader exists.
Field limits apply after parsing.
The create limiter runs after parsing.
counterevidence: Only JSON is accepted and fields are bounded.
Cloudflare request/isolate limits contain blast radius.
originalCandidates.recommended_remediation: Reject oversized declared bodies, use a bounded reader when absent, apply admission controls before parsing and enforce shallow schemas.

findings.title: Playback deduplication retains unbounded object identifiers per group
findings.summary: TrackPlayer records each group/object identifier before validating the audio envelope. PlaybackDeduplicator limits the number of groups to four but places every unique objectId in an uncapped Set, so one constant group grows for the player's lifetime.

severity.rationale: A malicious joined publisher can grow every automatically subscribed browser's heap indefinitely, including with malformed payloads that never reach playback.

confidence.rationale: The ordering and unbounded nested Set are direct source facts; normal 50-object cadence is not enforced.

codeEvidence.label: One group retains unlimited object IDs
codeEvidence.explanation: The group-count pruning does not bound entries within the Set.

codeEvidence.label: Identifiers are retained before payload validation
codeEvidence.explanation: Malformed objects still consume deduplication memory.

rootCause.summary: A group-count limit was mistaken for a total memory bound; per-group cardinality, bytes, cadence and malformed-object budgets are absent.

findings.remediation: Validate the envelope before retaining a dedupe key, cap identifiers per group and per track using expected cadence plus a burst margin, reject implausible progress and quarantine persistently malformed or over-budget tracks.

assertions: One Set accepts unlimited unique object IDs.
A constant group never triggers group pruning.
Malformed payloads are retained before decode failure.
counterEvidence: Closing or forgetting a player clears state.
Creating more than four groups prunes old groups.
External stream backpressure may reduce rate but does not cap retained entries.
limitations: A live browser exhaustion threshold was not measured.
validation.method: Offline source review of the exact authorised Git revision.

preconditions: The relay delivers the publisher's track to human subscribers.
steps: Join as a human publisher.
Hold groupId constant and vary objectId.
Send valid or malformed objects at high rate.

attackPath.summary: A malicious human publishes a high-rate same-group stream on their own track; automatic subscribers retain every new object ID before rejecting or decoding the payload.

remediationTests: Feed thousands of unique IDs in one group and assert fixed retained cardinality.
Repeat with malformed payloads and assert no dedupe growth.
Exceed the budget and assert track quarantine/unsubscription.

originalCandidates.rule: Unbounded per-group playback deduplication retains attacker-controlled object identifiers
originalCandidates.attacker: A malicious joined publisher using a modified client and the relay credential on its automatically subscribed human track, or a compromised relay.
originalCandidates.violated_security_invariant: Per-track receive state must have explicit object-count and byte bounds.
originalCandidates.source_to_sink: Relay group/object identifiers flow through MoqTransportAdapter and RoomSession to TrackPlayer.accept. PlaybackDeduplicator runs before envelope validation and adds every unique objectId to an unbounded Set. A constant groupId with varying objectId grows for TrackPlayer lifetime; repeated malformed objects do not quarantine the track.
originalCandidates.impact: A sustained same-group stream can grow the victim tab heap until UI/audio failure or tab termination.
supporting_source_evidence: Map<number, Set<number>> adds unbounded object IDs.
A single group never triggers four-group pruning.
Every other real human track is automatically subscribed.
No object-rate, byte-rate, malformed threshold or quarantine exists.
counterevidence: New distinct groups eventually prune older groups.
External flow control is not a retained-entry cap.
originalCandidates.recommended_remediation: Validate before deduplication; add per-track object and byte budgets, per-group identifier caps, progress checks and quarantine.

findings.title: Media bursts trigger count-unbounded sorting and decoder submission
findings.summary: Each valid frame entering AdaptiveJitterBuffer performs a linear duplicate scan, append, full sort and time-only prune. Arbitrarily many frames received within 200 ms survive, and TrackPlayer drains all eligible frames into AudioDecoder without a work or queue-depth budget.

severity.rationale: A malicious publisher can create superlinear main-thread work, retain many large frame copies and flood the decoder queue across automatically subscribed audience browsers.

confidence.rationale: The dynamic array operations and unlimited drain loop are direct source facts; the 200 ms time rule is not a count or byte bound.

codeEvidence.label: Every insert scans, sorts and time-prunes an unbounded array
codeEvidence.explanation: Many unique frames with near-identical receipt times evade stale pruning while causing repeated whole-array work.

codeEvidence.label: All eligible frames are submitted without a budget
codeEvidence.explanation: There is no per-drain frame count, time budget or AudioDecoder queue check.

rootCause.summary: Latency-only pruning was implemented without maximum frame count, byte count, cadence validation or decoder-work budgets, and an array-sort structure amplifies attacker-controlled bursts.

findings.remediation: Use a bounded sequence-indexed ring or heap, cap buffered objects and bytes, validate cadence/sequence/frame size, reject excess before sorting, limit work per drain, gate AudioDecoder.decode on decodeQueueSize and quarantine persistent offenders.

assertions: The buffer has no maximum frames or bytes.
Every insert executes some plus sort plus filter.
drain loops until no eligible frame remains and decodeFrame does not inspect decodeQueueSize.
counterEvidence: Frames older than 200 ms relative to a newer arrival are pruned.
Individual payload length, cancellation groups, concealment and mixer ring are bounded.
External Web Streams or relay flow control may reduce bursts.
limitations: The browser threshold and external relay backpressure were not measured.

Measure CPU and heap under an adversarial burst.

originalCandidates.rule: Count-unbounded jitter insertion and decoder submission permit algorithmic media-burst denial of service
originalCandidates.attacker: A malicious joined publisher sending valid unique envelopes far above the expected cadence, or a compromised relay.
originalCandidates.violated_security_invariant: The latency target must also impose count, byte and decode-work limits.
originalCandidates.source_to_sink: AdaptiveJitterBuffer scans, appends, sorts and time-filters a count-unbounded array on each valid object. Frames inside the 200 ms arrival window survive. drain submits all eligible frames to AudioDecoder without a work budget or decodeQueueSize check.
originalCandidates.impact: A short burst can cause superlinear main-thread work, retain many copied payloads and flood the decoder, causing audio/UI failure.
supporting_source_evidence: The 200 ms threshold is not a count bound.
Unique sequences with near-identical receive times survive.
One payload can be 65,535 bytes plus header.
No decoder-queue or inbound-rate degradation metric exists.
counterevidence: Mixer ring, cancelled groups, concealment and decoded AudioData lifetime are bounded.
External backpressure is not an application guarantee.
originalCandidates.recommended_remediation: Use a bounded sequence structure; cap objects/bytes; validate cadence and frame size; budget drains; gate decoder queue; quarantine persistent offenders.

findings.title: Unknown room-code probes initialise persistent SQLite Durable Objects
findings.summary: Any syntactically valid room code is mapped with getByName before existence is known. Constructing that Room always runs migrate, creating tables and schema_meta even though no room_meta row or cleanup alarm exists.

severity.rationale: An unauthenticated caller can generate unlimited valid-looking codes and create persistent object state outside the room-creation limiter, causing storage, billing or availability pressure.

confidence.rationale: The deterministic namespace mapping, constructor migration and persistent SQL writes are direct source facts; only the platform's precise cost is external.

codeEvidence.label: Every object construction migrates SQLite
codeEvidence.explanation: Unknown-room lookup invokes the same constructor as real room creation.

codeEvidence.label: Migration writes schema metadata
codeEvidence.explanation: The unknown object receives persistent SQLite schema state even though the room is never initialised.

rootCause.summary: Room-code existence is checked only after resolving the attacker-selected code into a stateful Durable Object whose constructor performs persistent migration.

findings.remediation: Validate a signed room capability or check a rate-limited room-code registry before getByName. Make unknown-room lookup non-writing and schedule cleanup or deletion for abandoned allocations.

assertions: The route regex accepts arbitrary valid-looking 20-character codes.
getByName is invoked before getSnapshot can return null.
The constructor always runs migrate and writes schema_meta.
No expiry alarm exists without room_meta.
counterEvidence: No room_meta, participant or relay credential is created.
Each schema is small.
Cloudflare storage lifecycle and billing are external.
limitations: The precise platform billing and quota impact was not verified.

originalCandidates.impact: Attackers can generate unlimited codes and create persistent SQLite-backed object schemas outside the creation limiter, causing storage, billing or availability pressure.

findings.title: Narrow read-only clients still start microphone capture and publication
findings.summary: The narrow layout is implemented as labels and CSS-hidden controls, but useRoomSession starts the same full RoomSession. RoomSession.start unconditionally invokes startPublishing, which requests getUserMedia and publishes frames when transport is live.

severity.rationale: A user told that the room is read-only can have microphone capture begin after joining and, where permission already exists and relay transport succeeds, transmit audio contrary to the product's mobile publishing boundary.

confidence.rationale: The getUserMedia and publication setup path is explicit. Actual narrow-browser relay publication was not reproduced and browser permission remains authoritative.

codeEvidence.label: Every room session starts publication
codeEvidence.explanation: No viewport or read-only policy prevents microphone startup.

codeEvidence.label: CaptureController requests the microphone
codeEvidence.explanation: Read-only presentation does not stop the privacy-sensitive API call.

rootCause.summary: Read-only capability is represented only in responsive presentation; it is not a session policy consumed by capture and publication code.

findings.remediation: Determine read-only mode before starting RoomSession, skip getUserMedia and publication entirely, stop capture if the configuration becomes read-only, and require a fresh explicit opt-in before enabling publishing.

assertions: Narrow UI says read-only and hides controls.
RoomSession.start always calls startPublishing.
CaptureController requests getUserMedia and live sessions publish encoded frames.
counterEvidence: The user explicitly joins.
Browser permission denial produces listen-only.
Relay transport is trace-unverified and unsupported devices may fail capture.
limitations: A real narrow browser with pre-granted permission was not exercised.
validation.method: Offline source review of the exact authorised Git revision.

remediationTests: On a narrow viewport, assert navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia is never called.
Assert no publication is created in read-only mode.
Transition into read-only and assert active capture and publication close.
Require explicit user opt-in before transitioning to publishing mode.
preventiveControls: Explicit capability model for publish versus read-only.
Privacy API tests across viewport/configuration matrix.

originalCandidates.rule: Narrow read-only clients still start microphone capture and publication
originalCandidates.attacker: A room inviter or participant inducing a narrow-screen user to join where microphone permission may already exist.
originalCandidates.violated_security_invariant: Narrow screens are read-only and must not capture or publish audio.
originalCandidates.source_to_sink: Entry does not block by viewport. CSS and RoomPage only present/hide controls as read-only, while useRoomSession creates a full RoomSession. RoomSession.start unconditionally starts publication; CaptureController requests microphone media and encoded frames publish once transport is live.
originalCandidates.impact: A narrow-screen user can have microphone capture start despite a read-only label; if permission is already granted and relay accepts, their audio is published.
supporting_source_evidence: RoomSession automatically starts publication on entry.

counterevidence: Unsupported capture may fail to listen-only.
originalCandidates.recommended_remediation: Make read-only an explicit policy before session start; skip getUserMedia and publication; stop capture on transition; require fresh opt-in to publish.

findings.title: Any participant can spoof another participant's activity
findings.summary: POST /active accepts a caller-selected targetId. markActive authenticates the caller but updates last_active_at for any matching participant without binding the target to the caller or a verified received track.

severity.rationale: A joined attendee can falsify audience-visible recency and participant ordering. The impact is limited to presentation integrity and does not directly change media routing or local degradation state.

confidence.rationale: The arbitrary target parameter and unrestricted update are explicit, while participant IDs are present in room snapshots.

codeEvidence.label: Authenticated caller selects any target
codeEvidence.explanation: Authentication proves only the caller; it does not authorise the caller-selected target.

rootCause.summary: The activity endpoint trusts a client assertion about who produced audio instead of deriving recency from an authenticated publication or track-observation capability.

findings.remediation: Remove the public arbitrary-target mutation. Derive activity from authenticated publication events, or require a capability proving the caller observed an authorised target track, and rate-limit reports.

assertions: Any valid participant credential passes authentication.
The target does not need to equal the caller.
Snapshots reveal valid target IDs and layout uses lastActiveAt.
counterEvidence: Unknown IDs cause a no-op.
No immediate broadcast occurs.
Local degradation uses locally observed object time.

remediationTests: Assert callers cannot update another participant's recency.

preventiveControls: Server-derived activity when the transport supports it.

originalCandidates.source_to_sink: POST /active accepts targetId; markActive authenticates the caller but updates any matching participant without binding the target to caller or observed track.
originalCandidates.impact: A participant can make known participants appear recently active and alter audience-visible prominence.
supporting_source_evidence: API accepts an asserted target.

counterevidence: Local degradation uses locally observed time.
originalCandidates.recommended_remediation: Remove arbitrary-target mutation and derive activity from authenticated publication or a capability proving the observed track.

candidate.rule: Open-room joining independently discloses the same relay-wide bearer without an issuance throttle
candidate.attacker: A holder of a valid room code.
candidate.violated_security_invariant: Open joining must not grant relay authority beyond the participant's permitted tracks and issuance must be throttled.
candidate.source_to_sink: POST /api/rooms/:code/join returns the same Worker token without a join or issuance limiter, together with snapshot identifiers used by deterministic track names.
candidate.impact: A room-code holder can obtain the bearer and target namespace inputs, then attempt routing bypass, unauthorised subscription or publication subject to relay semantics.
supporting_source_evidence: Join requires only room-code knowledge.
Every join receives the same credential.
Snapshot and deterministic naming expose namespace inputs.
No issuance budget exists.
counterevidence: Room codes are high entropy and rooms last at most twenty minutes.
Credential is absent from public snapshots and logs.
Relay acceptance and undocumented scope are unverified.
candidate.recommended_remediation: Mint a scoped credential after a controlled join; rate-limit issuance per source and room without imposing a participant-count cap.
